question: A 45-year-old woman presents with acute severe abdominal pain. An erect chest radiograph is requested to look for free intraperitoneal gas. The radiograph appears normal. Before concluding there is no pneumoperitoneum, what is the most important technical check the clinician should perform?

answers.text: Check whether the diaphragm is clearly visible bilaterally.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Partially correct — a clearly visible diaphragm is needed to exclude subdiaphragmatic gas — but the most important first check is confirming the patient was truly upright and the film was taken after adequate time for gas to accumulate under the diaphragm.

answers.text: Confirm that the film was taken with the patient fully erect and after waiting at least 5–10 minutes in that position, so that any free gas has had time to rise under the diaphragm.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Free intraperitoneal gas rises to the highest point. If the patient was not fully upright, or was moved to erect position immediately before the film, gas may not yet have risen to the subdiaphragmatic space and the film will be falsely negative. A film taken after the patient has been fully erect for at least 5–10 minutes is more reliable.

Incorrect. A contrast study is not the first-line response to a normal erect CXR when pneumoperitoneum is clinically suspected. The first step is ensuring correct film technique before concluding the film is truly negative.

answers.text: Request MRI abdomen as it is more sensitive for free gas.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. CT of the abdomen is the gold-standard cross-sectional investigation for pneumoperitoneum if clinical suspicion remains after a normal erect CXR. MRI is not routinely used for this indication in the emergency setting. However, before escalating, the film technique should be verified.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the governing principles of emergency film interpretation. Free gas on an erect film requires that the patient was actually upright for long enough for the gas to rise — always confirm correct positioning technique before concluding no pneumoperitoneum.
Correct. Before calling the erect CXR negative for free gas, confirm the patient was truly upright for at least 5–10 minutes.
